bullets.t: This is the Sacred Lake, a stone-lined pool dug for Thutmose III, about 128 metres by 83. Priests drew water here for ritual, and festival boats and the geese of Amun used it.
The water is groundwater, not a channel from the Nile. The lake is a pit cut into the water table, so it filled as the table rose with the yearly flood.
One engineers' study says it was fullest in November and almost dry by July, so the water was renewed every year. Since the High Dam levelled the groundwater, it has stagnated.
It is deep as well as wide: about four metres in the engineers' survey. Its sides are faced with stone, and stairs down to the water survive on the west, south and north sides.
Tradition says priests washed in it daily before ritual. Herodotus says Egyptian priests washed twice by day and twice by night, though he is describing priests in general, not this lake.
On the north side stood a building of Taharqa, about 690 BC, with a deep well. It looks like a Nilometer, but it seems to have been ritual, linking the temple to the primeval waters.
Sizes differ by source: Digital Karnak says 128 by 83 metres, the engineers' survey about 130 by 80. Either way it is larger than a football pitch.

kids.t: Find the tall palm trees beside the water and count them.

lake.look: The big rectangular stone-lined pool, about 128 by 83 metres (Digital Karnak), with palm trees beside it.
lake.note: Open to visitors; the café is on its north-west side. Little shade, and the light is best early. Keep a firm hold of your daughter near the edge: the sides are stone steps.

bullets.t: Look back across the water from here. The lake is in front, the temple rises beyond it to the north-west, and the still surface doubles the view. Reviewers call this the most atmospheric corner.
The Egyptians saw a temple lake as the primeval water from which the world rose. The well on the far bank, next to Taharqa's building, was thought to reach down to it.
On the far bank stood Taharqa's building, 25 metres wide and 29 deep. Only 1 to 2.5 metres of wall survive, so you see low foundations rather than a temple.
The lake needed no pump. It sits in the water table, which the study says rose and fell about 0.8 metres a year with the Nile flood, and so refilled it.

kids.t: Wave to the palm trees in the water: find their reflection.

lakeview.look: From the south-east corner, point the camera north-west: the water in front, the temple behind.
lakeview.note: Little shade. If the corner is crowded, any bank of the lake gives a similar view.

bullets.t: This is the Cachette Court. From December 1903 Georges Legrain dug a deep pit here and found hundreds of buried statues. The work ran in four seasons, to July 1907.
Counts vary. Legrain's first season gave 457 statues. By 1905 Maspero reported seven hundred, and popular totals say 750 to 800, with 17,000 or more small bronzes.
They date from the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemies. Legrain thought the pit was filled in one go, in the Greek period. Nobody recorded why. Retiring old sacred statues is the usual guess.

Water was the enemy. The pit lay below the water table, so workers lifted it out with shadufs, hand-swung bucket levers, to about ten metres, later nearly fourteen. Maspero called it fishing for statues.
The bronzes are a mystery. Legrain counted about 17,000, yet they seem to have vanished from the records since. Maspero cut the bronzes from his own account when he reprinted it in 1914.
Behind the court is the Seventh Pylon, 26 metres high, built for Thutmose III. The scene of him smiting captives is on its south face, so you need to pass through to see it.
On the court's west wall is Ramesses II's treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III, from about 1259 BC. Neither would attack the other, and each would help if a third power did.
The Hittite side survives on clay tablets in Akkadian, found at Hattusa in Turkey from 1906. Two are in Istanbul and one in Berlin. A copy is said to hang at the United Nations, unconfirmed.
Four carved battle scenes flank the treaty. They were once given to Ramesses II, but are now identified as episodes from his son Merneptah's Canaanite campaign.

kids: Spot the little birds and snakes carved in the long wall of hieroglyphs.
cachette.look: The open court south of the Hypostyle Hall, with the Seventh Pylon at its south end. The long wall of hieroglyphs on the west side is the treaty.
cachette.note: Reached from the south side of the Hypostyle Hall. The way on beyond the Seventh Pylon may be closed; if so, see the pylon's north face from the court and the treaty wall from the court's west side.

bullets.t: South of the Seventh Pylon, Karnak's southern road runs through three more gateways, the Eighth, Ninth and Tenth Pylons, towards the Temple of Mut and on to Luxor.
The Eighth was begun under Hatshepsut: 21 metres high, 47.7 long, sandstone. Later kings recarved most of her work. It is the oldest on this road, but Thutmose I's Fourth Pylon is older.
Horemheb built the Ninth, 26 metres high, and finished the Tenth that Amenhotep III left at its lowest courses. Both pylons are partly filled with blocks from Akhenaten's dismantled temples.
The Tenth Pylon has a rose granite doorway 15.6 metres high. Its court shows Horemheb's voyage to Punt, and the treasure he brought back.
Reliefs between the Eighth and Ninth show the Opet festival: the god's boat carried by priests, setting out on its journey south to Luxor.

kids.t: Count the giant gateways in a row. How many can you see?

southpylons.look: The line of gateways south of the Cachette Court: the Eighth nearest, then the Ninth, with the Tenth behind.
southpylons.note: May be closed; if so, see the Seventh Pylon from the Cachette Court and look south through its gate. Two older accounts say most of the area beyond the Eighth Pylon was closed, but photographers recorded all three pylons on 10 March 2024 and 4 December 2025.

bullets.t: This is the Temple of Khonsu, the moon god, son of Amun and Mut. It is a small but complete New Kingdom temple: pylon, open court, columned hall, bark chamber and sanctuary.
Khonsu's name means traveller, for the moon crossing the night sky. He was also a healer. One Egyptian story has him as the reborn sun, son of Amun.
Ramesses III (reigned 1184 to 1153 BC) began it, using fresh stone and old blocks from Eighteenth Dynasty buildings. A column drum in the court still carries Horemheb's cartouche.
Ramesses XI and the High Priest Herihor built the front. Herihor later took royal titles, and the family procession on the portico wall is his, as the Epigraphic Survey records.
Unlike much of Karnak, the hall and rooms still carry their stone roof, so it is dim. A stair leads up to the roof, where a solar chapel was cut.
Taharqa added a porch of twenty papyrus columns in front of the pylon, about 690 BC. Stone beams joined them; stone slabs would have been too heavy, so the roof was probably timber.
Next door, to the west, is the little Temple of Opet. In the myth, Amun dies as Osiris and is reborn through the goddess Opet. Her temple faces a door of this one.
Opet's temple has crypts sunk into its platform, including a tomb of Osiris and a birth chamber. It stands on a podium 19.6 by 22.7 metres, and is often locked.
South of the temple stands the Bab el-Amara, a 21-metre stone gateway of Ptolemy III. The pylon towers beside it were begun by Nectanebo I and never finished.

kids.t: Find the monkey: the moon god Khonsu is carved as a baboon in the columned hall.

khonsu.look: The pylon and the open court with its 28 papyrus-bud columns, then the dim columned hall behind.
khonsu.note: Steps at the entrance. The interior may be partly closed: one account found much of it roped off, others walked in and saw the ceiling and painted reliefs. If so, see the pylon, court and colonnade from the doorway. The Opet temple may be locked; if so, see it from the side.
